description: House conventions for Jira, covering issue types and hierarchy, summary form, description structure, acceptance criteria, priority and labels, and the boundary between what a ticket owns and what belongs in a pull request or an architecture record. Use when reading, writing, judging, or reorganising Jira issues, or when deciding which issue type a piece of work should be. For the act of drafting or filing one use writing-jira-tickets, and for Linear use linear-conventions.
# Jira conventions
A Jira ticket exists for people who will not read the code. A lead reads it to plan, and managers
read it to decide whether the work is worth doing. It is the durable answer to why a piece of work
exists and what changes, and that audience is why the conventions below keep it short and keep
implementation detail out of it entirely.
The routing test: **would this sentence be false once the pull request merges?** If yes, it belongs
in the pull request, not the ticket. "The guard now checks status before method" goes stale on merge.
"Users see a stale score after automation runs" stays true as a record of why the work happened.
Every site configures Jira differently. Read the project's real issue types, fields and workflow
from the API before relying on any list here, because an invented field name fails at create time
and an invented convention is worse, since it will be copied.
## Issue types
The standard agile set. Confirm against the project before use.
| Type | Use when | Not for |
| `Epic` | A body of work spanning several tickets, holding shared context and links | A single deliverable |
| `Story` | User-visible capability, described from the user's side | Internal work with no user facing it |
| `Task` | Engineering work that must happen but has no user story | Anything a user would describe |
| `Bug` | Behaviour that contradicts intent, with reproduction steps | Work that was never built |
| `Spike` | A timeboxed question, delivering a recommendation rather than code | Work whose approach is already known |
| `Sub-task` | A slice of one parent that is not independently deliverable | Work another team could pick up alone |
Hierarchy runs epic, then story, task, bug and spike, then sub-task. Some sites add levels above
epic for roadmap planning, and those are usually owned by a planning process rather than by
engineers. Test-management plugins add their own types; leave them to the process that owns them.
**Type is not severity and not effort.** A one-line fix is still a bug, and a large bug is still a
bug rather than a story.
## Summary
The summary is read in a list of fifty, so it carries the whole ticket for most people who see it.
- Imperative, starting with a verb. `Reject expired session tokens`, not `Session token issue`.
- Specific enough that two engineers cannot read it differently. If they can, rewrite it.
- Searchable: include the noun someone would search for six months from now.
- No type prefix. The type is a field, and `Bug: ` in the summary duplicates it.
- Bracket prefixes cost more than they give. One is tolerable where a site already relies on it;
`[Area] [Thing] [Action] Real summary` is a file list wearing a label and it destroys scannability.
- For a bug, name the who, what and where rather than reaching for a generic verb:
`Links in related documents do not trigger a download`.
| Weak | Why | Better |
| `Fix login bug` | True of many tickets | `Log in fails silently when the session token expires` |
| `Improve performance` | Unfalsifiable | `Cut dashboard load below two seconds on 4G` |
| `Update the parser` | Names an area, not a change | `Accept quoted field names in the CSV parser` |
| `Changes after review` | Describes the workflow | Describe what the work now does |
## Description
Two parts. Nothing else.
1. **The problem**, in two or three sentences of plain language, including what it costs. Someone
who has never opened the repository should understand it, because a lead and managers read these
and neither of them will open the repository.
2. **`Done when:`**, with two or three outcome lines.
Around 80 words, with 100 as a ceiling. For a bug, the problem sentences carry how to see it. For a
spike, replace `Done when:` with the question, the timebox and the deliverable.
**No identifiers.** No file paths, symbol or table names, line numbers, commit hashes, or branch
names. **No technical notes section.** Implementation detail belongs in a comment, where the person
doing the work looks and nobody else has to scroll past it. Moving detail to the bottom of a
description is not the same as leaving it out, and it reads just as badly.
Keep the one number that makes the case, such as how long something has been broken or how large it
has grown. Drop the rest, especially breakdowns by cause.
Keep it factual. Discussion belongs in comments, and a decision reached in a comment gets folded
back into the description, because nobody reads forty comments to find the current requirement.
**Do not restate what Jira already renders.** The type, status, assignee, priority, sprint, parent
and link list are all on the screen. Prose repeating any of it is pure cost.
## Acceptance criteria
Two or three lines under `Done when:`, each **one observable outcome**. Not a checklist, and not the
implementation plan.
A line passes if someone who did not do the work can tell whether it holds. It fails if it names a
file, a flag or a function, because that is a step rather than an outcome.
| Weak | Why | Better |
| Works correctly | Nobody can check it | Expired sessions are rejected instead of accepted |
| Performance is improved | Unfalsifiable | The page loads in under two seconds |
| Add the strict flag to the pipeline | A step, not an outcome | A new warning fails the build |
| Refactor the module | Describes activity | The existing tests pass unchanged |
If you need eight lines, the ticket is too big, or you are writing the implementation plan in the
wrong place.
## Fields
- **Priority reflects business impact, not effort.** A trivial fix to a broken payment path is high
priority. A hard, nice-to-have refactor is not.
- **Labels stay few and mean something.** A label applied once is noise, and a label duplicating a
field is worse. Read the existing set before adding a new one.
- **Components and fix versions** are only useful where a team actually filters on them. Do not
populate a field because it is there.
- **Estimates** describe effort, never importance.
## What a ticket does not own
| Content | Where it belongs |
| What the diff does, file by file | The pull request |
| Permanent architectural rationale | An architecture decision record, see `writing-adrs` |
| The tracker ID itself, repeated in commits | Nowhere. It lives in the branch name and the pull request title |
| Status narration once work starts | The workflow state, not the description |
| A conversation | An actual conversation. Jira used as a chat channel is the most common failure |
Requirements that change substantially after work starts are a new ticket, not an edit. Rewriting a
description mid-sprint invalidates the estimate and the review everyone already did.
## Boundary with other trackers
Where a project uses Linear, `linear-conventions` and `tracking-work-in-linear` own it and this
skill does not apply. Where GitHub Issues carries engineering work under a tracker item, see
`github-issue-conventions`. One piece of work gets one home; the others link to it.
## Maintenance
These conventions describe practice, not any one site's configuration. When a project's real setup
disagrees with something here, the project wins for that project, and the disagreement is worth
recording where the team will see it rather than editing this file to match one installation.

name: writing-jira-tickets

description: Decides whether a Jira ticket is worth creating, then drafts, splits, or rewrites it so that someone outside the project can understand it. Covers summaries, acceptance criteria, spikes with a timebox, when to split, and creating issues through an Atlassian MCP server. Use when asked to file, draft, split, or improve a Jira ticket, when asked whether something is worth tracking, or when follow-up work surfaces mid-task and needs a home. For Linear use tracking-work-in-linear, and for GitHub Issues use writing-github-issues.
# Writing Jira tickets
A ticket is a work order for a reader who was not in the conversation that produced it. Most of the
craft is removing what only makes sense to the person writing it.
Conventions live in `jira-conventions`. Invoke it if it is not already loaded, and read the project's
real issue types and fields from the API rather than assuming any default set.
## First, does it deserve a ticket
**"No ticket needed" is a correct answer, and a common one.** A backlog nobody trusts is worse than
a short one, and every ticket costs refinement time, a status nobody updates, and a search result
that wastes someone's afternoon in a year.
| Do this | When |
| Nothing | It is an observation, or it will be obvious again when it matters |
| Fix it now | It is smaller than the ticket describing it |
| Say it in the pull request | It only concerns the change under review |
| A comment on an existing ticket | Someone already owns the surrounding work |
| A new ticket | The work is real, separable, and will otherwise be forgotten |
Do not default to the last row. This is advice, not a veto: if the user asks for a ticket, write one
and say if you think it is not needed.
## Three modes, and which one you are in
| Mode | Produces | Authorised by |
| Draft | Text in the conversation | Nothing. Always available |
| Propose | A recommendation on type, summary, criteria, and whether to file at all | Nothing |
| Write | A created or edited issue | An explicit instruction to create or update it |
**Default to propose.** "Can you make a ticket for that" is a request for a draft, not for a write
to the tracker. A better version of an existing description is not authorisation to save it.
## Before writing anything, read
1. **The work itself.** The diff, the failing test, the code path. A ticket written from a
conversation about the work, rather than from the work, is where invented detail enters.
2. **The project's configuration.** Issue types, required fields, and whether a parent is expected.
3. **Existing tickets.** Search before creating. A duplicate is indistinguishable from the original
within a week, and both then get worked.
4. **The linked context**, where one exists: the epic, the decision record, the incident.
**Verify a path, symbol, or number before naming it.** An invented fact in a tracker is
indistinguishable from a real one, and it will be acted on. This is the one area where being vague
is cheaper than being wrong: write "several hundred lines" rather than guessing "700".
## Writing it
**A ticket is read by a lead and by managers, not by the person implementing it.** That single fact
decides everything below. Someone who cannot open the repository has to understand what is wrong and
why it is worth a sprint. If they cannot, the ticket has failed no matter how accurate it is.
The shape, every time:
<two or three sentences naming the problem and its cost>
Done when:
- <outcome>
- <outcome>
**Around 80 words. One hundred is a ceiling, not a target.** Past that you are narrating, and the
reader has stopped.
- **No identifiers anywhere in the description.** No file paths, no symbol or table names, no line
numbers, no commit hashes, no branch names. Not lower down either: there is no lower down. A
description that opens with a procedure name and a guard condition is unreadable to most of its
audience, and relocating that text to a notes section at the bottom does not fix it.
- **No technical notes section.** Implementation detail goes in the first comment, where the person
doing the work will look and nobody else has to scroll past it.
- **`Done when:` lines are outcomes, not steps.** "The build prints no warnings" passes. "Add the
strict flag to the workflow" is a step, and naming a file is the tell. Two or three lines. If you
need eight, the ticket is too big or you are writing the implementation plan.
- **Keep the one number that makes the case.** "Failing for a month" and "781 lines" justify the
work to a manager in a way that "some problems" never will. Drop every other number, especially
breakdowns by cause.
- **Expand an acronym on first use, or cut it.** Project shorthand is opaque even inside the team.
- **Say what is wrong, not how to fix it.** The fix is a proposal review may change. Put an approach
in the comment, marked as a suggestion.
Cut anything unfalsifiable. "Improves maintainability", "ensures robustness", "various
improvements", "this ticket introduces" are claims nobody can check or formulas delaying the
content. Replace with what will specifically be true, or delete.
Run the description through `humanizer` before showing it. Ticket prose attracts the same generated
tics as any other writing, and an em dash standing in for a colon is the most common one.
## Spikes
A spike needs three things, and is not ready without all of them.
- **One question.** Not a topic and not a list. "Should the scoring rules move into the
transformation layer" is a question; "investigate the scoring architecture" is not.
- **A timebox**, stated in the ticket. Hours or days, rarely more than a sprint.
- **A named deliverable.** A recommendation, a prototype, a benchmark, a decision note. A spike
whose deliverable is "understanding" cannot be finished, and it will sit open for a quarter.
Write the acceptance criterion as the deliverable existing, not as the question being answered
correctly, because the answer may legitimately be "we cannot tell yet".
## Splitting
Split along seams where each piece is independently deliverable and separately valuable. A ticket
that produces nothing until its sibling lands is a sub-task, not a ticket.
Do not split to make an estimate smaller, and do not split work whose halves cannot ship
independently. A migration that breaks the application halfway through is one ticket.
## Editing an existing ticket
1. **Read the current version and the work it describes** before changing a word.
2. **Update the description when it no longer matches reality**, not when you would have phrased it
differently.
3. **Fold decisions out of comments** into the description, where the next reader will find them.
4. **Leave the chronology in the comments.** The description holds the current requirement, not its
history.
5. **Change the type** when it is wrong, and say why.
6. **Do not rewrite requirements mid-sprint.** Substantial change is a new ticket.
**Leaving it alone is a result.** A description that is accurate, current, and proportionate gets
left alone, and saying so is the right answer. Rewriting a good ticket churns the page, buries the
notification, and teaches people to ignore updates.
## Tool surface
An Atlassian MCP server exposes these as `mcp__atlassian__*`. Discover the site rather than
hardcoding one:
- `getAccessibleAtlassianResources` returns the `cloudId` every other call needs.
- `getJiraProjectIssueTypesMetadata` gives the project's real types before you pick one.
- `searchJiraIssuesUsingJql` for the duplicate check.
- `createJiraIssue` takes `contentFormat: "markdown"` and a `description` string. Fields without
their own parameter, including `priority`, `labels` and `components`, go in `additional_fields`.
- `editJiraIssue` for an update.
Never hardcode a cloud ID, project key, or epic key into a skill or a reusable script. If no server
is available, produce the summary and description as markdown for someone to paste, and say that is
what you did rather than implying it was filed.
Markdown is converted to Atlassian Document Format on the way in, and the conversion is lossy in
at least one way worth knowing: **a list item containing backticks makes the converter downgrade the
whole `- [ ]` list to escaped literal text**, so the checkboxes arrive as `* \[ \]` on the page.
Verified on a real site. Plain bullets do not have this problem, which is another reason `Done when:`
uses them.
So after creating or editing, fetch the issue back and confirm the description rendered. A mangled
list is invisible from the create response, which returns only a key.
## The preview
Before any write, show the exact text: issue type, summary, the full description, and any field you
intend to set. One ticket per preview, not a summary of four.
**Count the words and say the number.** It is the one check that catches the most common failure
before it reaches the tracker, and it takes a second.
## Before you finish
- The ticket exists for a stated reason, or you recommended not creating one.
- The first sentence is comprehensible to someone who has never opened the repository, and makes
the case for doing the work.
- No identifier appears anywhere in the description.
- The description is under one hundred words, and you counted.
- There is no technical notes section, and any implementation detail is in a comment.
- Every `Done when:` line is an outcome rather than a step.
- A spike has a question, a timebox, and a deliverable.
- Every path, symbol and number was verified, and anything uncertain is marked as uncertain.
- A duplicate search ran before creating.
- No site-specific key, ID or label vocabulary was hardcoded.
- Nothing was created or edited without approval.
